questions.q: List the five components of a Computerised Accounting System as per NCERT Class 12.
questions.a:
Correct answer: Procedure, Data, People, Hardware, Software.  
A wrong answer (e.g., listing "Reports", "Ledger", "Trial Balance") reveals the student confuses *outputs* of CAS with its *structural components*. Reports are generated *by* the system; they are not pillars the system rests on.

questions.q: A student says: "Hardware is the most important component because without a computer you cannot run CAS." Explain why this statement is incomplete using the concept of interdependence among the five components.
questions.a:
Correct explanation: Hardware alone cannot process accounting transactions — it needs Software to instruct it, Data to process, Procedures to define the workflow, and People to operate and interpret results. Removing any one component collapses the system.  
A wrong answer (e.g., agreeing without qualification) shows the student views components in isolation rather than as an integrated socio-technical system, a key NCERT emphasis.

questions.q: A retail shop uses Tally on a desktop. The accountant enters a credit sale of ₹12,000 to M/s Sharma Traders. Identify which component of CAS corresponds to: (a) the voucher entry screen, (b) the accountant, (c) the rule "credit sales go through Sales Voucher", (d) the desktop, (e) the ₹12,000 figure.
questions.a:
(a) Software (application interface), (b) People, (c) Procedure, (d) Hardware, (e) Data.  
A wrong mapping (e.g., calling the voucher screen "Procedure") indicates the student cannot distinguish between the *tool* (software) and the *rules* (procedure) — a common confusion when first learning CAS architecture.

questions.q: Compare the role of "Procedure" in a manual accounting system versus a computerised one. Why does NCERT list Procedure as a separate component in CAS when it exists in manual systems too?
questions.a:
In manual systems, procedures are implicit habits (e.g., "write in journal then post to ledger"). In CAS, procedures must be *explicitly coded* into software workflows (voucher types, mandatory fields, validation rules). NCERT separates Procedure because CAS forces formalisation — you cannot "skip a step" as you might manually.  
A wrong answer (e.g., "procedure is same in both") misses the critical shift from tacit to explicit, codified logic — a core idea for understanding why CAS reduces errors.

questions.q: Evaluate this claim: "Data is the only component that changes with every transaction; the other four remain static." Defend or refute with two specific examples.
questions.a:
Refute. Data changes per transaction (correct). But Software changes via updates/patches; Hardware changes via upgrades/failures; People change via training/turnover; Procedures change via policy revisions (e.g., GST rate change alters voucher entry procedure).  
A wrong answer (agreeing) reveals a static view of CAS — dangerous for real-world implementation where all components evolve.

questions.q: Design a minimal CAS for a freelance graphic designer who receives 5–10 payments a month and has 3–4 recurring expenses. Specify one concrete choice for each of the five components (e.g., Hardware: smartphone; Software: Wave Apps; etc.) and justify why that choice fits the scale.
questions.a:
Example answer:  
- Hardware: Smartphone (portable, already owned)  
- Software: Wave Apps (free, cloud-based, mobile-friendly)  
- People: Designer herself (sole user)  
- Data: Bank SMS alerts + manual entry of expense receipts  
- Procedure: Weekly 15-min session: reconcile bank → categorise → generate P&L  
Justification: Low volume, zero budget, mobile-first — each component matches the scale.  
A poor answer (e.g., recommending Tally on a server) shows inability to match CAS architecture to business context — a key competency for board case studies.
